## What you will learn

- Bring Nav2 up on karmel itself, with the right clock, the right map and the LiDAR driver, and verify each layer before the wheels touch the floor.
- Measure the six numbers that decide every Nav2 parameter on your robot, instead of copying a TurtleBot's.
- Turn those measurements into specific parameter changes with a calculation for each one.
- Diagnose the four failures that only happen on hardware: doorways, slip, localization jitter and a starved CPU.
- Run a first autonomous errand safely and know what stops the robot when your software does not.

## Why it matters

The simulation gave you a robot with perfect wheels, a noiseless LiDAR, unlimited CPU and a map that matches the world exactly. Your flat gives you none of those, plus a cat. Nav2's defaults were tuned for a TurtleBot 3 or 4 in a lab: 0.22 m radius, 0.5 m/s, a laptop-class CPU. karmel is 25 × 21 cm, cruises at 0.25 m/s and runs everything on a Raspberry Pi 5 that is also doing AMCL and the LiDAR driver.

This lesson is where the course stops being about algorithms and becomes about *your* robot in *your* home. Every parameter you change here must have a number behind it, and that number must come from a measurement — which is the whole method, and it transfers to every robot you ever tune.

## Concept

### Six ways the real robot is not the simulation

| | Simulation | Your flat |
|---|---|---|
| Clock | `/clock` from Gazebo; every node needs `use_sim_time:=true` | the system clock; `use_sim_time` must be **false** everywhere |
| LiDAR | exact ranges, exact 10 Hz, no dropouts | noise, reflections off glass and gloss-white doors, missing returns, 8–12 Hz jitter |
| Wheel odometry | exact integration of the commanded twist | slip on rugs, wheel-radius error, caster drag ([09.05](../09-odometry/09.05-calibrating-odometry.md)) |
| Obstacles | in the world file, or not at all | cables, socks, chair legs — all below the 16.5 cm scan plane |
| CPU | as much as your laptop has | a Pi 5 also running SLAM/AMCL and the LiDAR driver |
| Failure | reset the simulation | the robot hits your wall; wheels off the ground for the first tests |

Five of the six make the robot *less* certain of where it is and what is around it. That is the theme of every change you will make: on a real robot, the parameters that assume precision have to be relaxed, and the ones that assume time have to be shortened.

### Measure, then tune. Never the other way round

The failure mode of everybody's first real-robot Nav2 is a parameter file full of changes nobody can justify, none of which can be undone because nobody remembers what they fixed. The discipline is dull and it works:

1. **Measure six numbers** on the robot, driving, in the room it will live in: the scan rate, the controller rate the software actually achieves, AMCL's pose noise while standing still, the age of the newest TF, the narrowest doorway, and the speed the robot really reaches when told 0.25 m/s.
2. **Compute** what each number implies, with the arithmetic in this lesson.
3. **Change one parameter**, re-run the *same* goal, write down what happened.
4. Keep a diff, not a new file. Five justified lines beat a rewritten YAML.

[`code/tuning.py`](code/tuning.py) does step 2 for you: it takes your measurements and prints the specific parameter changes with the reason attached.

> [!TIP]
> **Ask your teacher:** "Quiz me: give me a measurement from a real robot and ask which Nav2 parameter it changes and by how much."

### The robot does not stop because your program stops

Before anything drives: on karmel there are four independent things that stop the wheels, and your navigation software is the *least* reliable of them.

```text
Nav2 controller  ->  velocity smoother  ->  collision monitor  ->  diff_drive_controller  ->  Pico firmware
   (goal logic)      (accel limits,          (sensor reflex,        (cmd_vel timeout        (watchdog: 300 ms
                      velocity_timeout)       12.10)                 0.5 s)                  without a command
                                                                                             -> motors off)
```

Only the last one keeps working when the Pi crashes, the Wi-Fi drops or your Python throws. That is why the firmware watchdog of [01.10](../01-first-robot/01.10-pi-pico-protocol.md) exists, and why you test it before the first autonomous run, every time.

> [!CAUTION]
> **Safety:** the first autonomous run is the one that surprises you. Wheels off the ground on a stand for the first goal; a reachable power switch or e-stop in your hand for the second; people, pets and cables out of the test area; `desired_linear_vel` at 0.15 m/s until the robot has completed ten goals without touching anything. Verify the watchdog: with the robot on the stand and driving, kill the navigation process and confirm the wheels stop within a few hundred milliseconds. ([SAFETY.md](../SAFETY.md))

## Technical explanation

### Level 1 — Bringing it up on hardware

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Version-sensitive** (verified 2026-09 against ROS 2 Jazzy on Ubuntu 24.04, Nav2 1.3.13, Raspberry Pi 5; the Nav2 side is the same workspace as [12.07](12.07-nav2-in-simulation.md), the hardware paths were verified against a fake Pico, see [labs/ros2_ws/TESTED.md](../labs/ros2_ws/TESTED.md)).
> Check the current driver and Nav2 docs before installing: https://docs.nav2.org/jazzy/configuration_and_development/first_time_robot_setup_guide/
> AI teacher: verify against current documentation before giving instructions.

On the Pi, one layer at a time, checking each:

```bash
# 1. the robot: ros2_control + the Pico over serial          (08.12)
ros2 launch karmel_bringup robot.launch.py sim:=false
ros2 control list_controllers          # joint_state_broadcaster + diff_drive_controller active
ros2 topic hz /odom                    # ~50 Hz

# 2. the LiDAR driver                                        (07.11)
ros2 launch sllidar_ros2 sllidar_c1_launch.py
ros2 topic hz /scan                    # this number goes into your measurements

# 3. a map of the room, and localization in it               (11.07, 10.09)
ros2 launch karmel_bringup navigation.launch.py \
     map:=$HOME/maps/my_home.yaml use_sim_time:=false
# then RViz "2D Pose Estimate", or initial_pose:=true x:=… y:=… yaw:=…

# 4. goals                                                   (12.07, 12.09)
```

Three things bite here and nowhere else:

- **`use_sim_time:=false`, everywhere.** `navigation.launch.py` defaults it to `true` for the simulation. One node left on simulated time sees a clock stuck at zero, every TF lookup is "too far in the past", and you get `TF_ERROR` with no hint of the cause.
- **The scan frame and the mounting.** `laser` must be where the LiDAR physically is, to the centimetre, and rotated the way it is actually bolted on. A LiDAR mounted 180° out gives a map that looks fine and localization that is confidently wrong ([05.08](../05-frames-and-transforms/05.08-urdf-and-xacro.md)).
- **The map is now yours.** Walls are a few centimetres thick and slightly wavy, furniture that moved between mapping and driving is wrong, and there is unknown space behind everything ([11.09](../11-slam/11.09-slam-troubleshooting.md)).

### Level 2 — The six measurements

Do these with the robot on the floor, in the room, after a two-minute warm-up.

| # | Measure | How | Feeds |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | scan rate | `ros2 topic hz /scan` while driving | `transform_tolerance`, the latency budget |
| 2 | controller rate | `controller_server` log: "Control loop missed its desired rate" — count per minute; or `ros2 topic hz /cmd_vel_nav` | `controller_frequency`, whether MPPI is even possible |
| 3 | AMCL pose noise | stand still 30 s, `ros2 topic echo /amcl_pose --field pose.covariance`; take $\sigma = \sqrt{C_{xx}}$ | `xy_goal_tolerance`, `update_min_d` |
| 4 | TF age | `ros2 run tf2_ros tf2_monitor map base_footprint` | `transform_tolerance` |
| 5 | narrowest doorway | a tape measure, at the narrowest point including the door frame and the skirting board | `inflation_radius`, `cost_scaling_factor`, `lookahead_dist` |
| 6 | actual top speed | command 0.25 m/s for 3 m, time it (or read `/odom`) | `desired_linear_vel` |

Plus one you already know: the CPU load on the Pi with everything running (`top -H`, or `htop`).

### Level 3 — From a measurement to a parameter, with the arithmetic

**Doorways and inflation.** A cell is `INSCRIBED_INFLATED_OBSTACLE` (253, which planners refuse) within the **inscribed radius**, not within `inflation_radius`. karmel's costmap footprint is 0.25 × 0.21 m plus 1 cm padding, so the inscribed radius is $r = 0.115$ m and the free corridor through a door of width $w$ is

$$c = w - 2r$$

For an 80 cm door: $c = 0.8 - 0.23 = 0.57$ m. The *cost* in the middle of the door comes from the inflation formula of [12.04](12.04-costmaps.md):

$$\text{cost} = \left\lfloor 252\, e^{-k\,(d - r)} \right\rfloor, \qquad d = w/2$$

With $k = 5$ and $d = 0.4$: $252\,e^{-5(0.285)} = 60$. Passable and cheap. The same door with Nav2's default `inflation_radius: 0.70` and `cost_scaling_factor: 3.0` would still be geometrically passable — inflation radius never blocks — but the whole corridor would cost 120–200, and Regulated Pure Pursuit's cost-regulated speed scaling would crawl through it. `tuning.py` prints the table:

```text
doorways
    door 60 cm: half-gap 30.0 cm, clearance +18.5 cm, cost at the centre 99 -> passable
    door 70 cm: half-gap 35.0 cm, clearance +23.5 cm, cost at the centre 77 -> passable
    door 80 cm: half-gap 40.0 cm, clearance +28.5 cm, cost at the centre 60 -> passable
    door 90 cm: half-gap 45.0 cm, clearance +33.5 cm, cost at the centre 47 -> passable
```

**The corner cut.** A pure-pursuit arc toward a carrot $L$ ahead passes about $L(1-\cos(\theta/2))$ inside a corner of angle $\theta$; for 90° that is $0.293\,L$. With `lookahead_dist: 0.4` that is 11.7 cm. Compare it with the clearance $c/2$ on each side: in a 60 cm doorway you have 18.5 cm, so 0.4 m of lookahead is fine but 0.8 m (23.4 cm of cut) is not.

**Stopping distance, with latency.** The part people forget:

$$d_{\text{stop}} = \underbrace{v\,(T_{\text{sensor}} + T_{\text{costmap}} + T_{\text{controller}})}_{\text{blind}} + \underbrace{\frac{v^2}{2a}}_{\text{braking}}$$

karmel at 0.25 m/s with a 10 Hz LiDAR, a 5 Hz local costmap, a 20 Hz controller and `max_decel: -0.8`:

```text
    0.25 m/s: blind    8.8 cm (350 ms of latency) + braking  3.9 cm =  12.7 cm   -> local costmap >= 0.9 m
    0.50 m/s: blind   17.5 cm (350 ms of latency) + braking 15.6 cm =  33.1 cm   -> local costmap >= 1.3 m
```

At karmel's speed **latency dominates braking more than two to one**. Raising the LiDAR rate or the costmap rate buys more than stronger brakes — and the 2 × 2 m local costmap has plenty of margin, which is why it can stay small and cheap.

**Goal tolerance.** A tolerance below your localization noise plus your overshoot is never reliably met:

$$\text{tolerance} \ge 2\sigma_{\text{AMCL}} + v\,T_{\text{latency}} + \text{margin}$$

With $\sigma = 2$ cm (a good day on a small LiDAR robot) that is $0.04 + 0.088 + 0.03 = 0.158$ m — which is why karmel ships 0.15 and why a robot with 8 cm of AMCL jitter needs 0.28 m and will look sloppy.

**TF tolerance.** Cover about three periods of the slowest thing in the chain: at 10 Hz, 0.3 s. karmel ships `transform_tolerance: 0.2`, which is tight for a real 10 Hz LiDAR — `tuning.py` flags it even for a healthy robot.

**Compute.** On a Pi 5 running AMCL, the LiDAR driver and two costmaps, the controller is the thing with a deadline. Regulated Pure Pursuit is a handful of geometric operations per cycle; MPPI at Nav2's defaults is 1000 trajectories × 56 steps at 20–30 Hz. That is the reasoning written at the top of karmel's [`nav2_params.yaml`](../labs/ros2_ws/src/karmel_bringup/config/nav2_params.yaml), and it is why the CPU measurement comes before the controller choice, not after.

### Level 4 — The four failures that are hardware-only

**1. The doorway that closes.** Verified in [12.07](12.07-nav2-in-simulation.md): the global costmap's obstacle layer, marking LiDAR returns out to 3.5 m, places them with the full localization error and closes an 80 cm door for the planner. On hardware this is *worse*, because AMCL's error is larger. Shorten the **global** `obstacle_max_range` to something your localization can support (1.5 m is a reasonable start) and leave the local costmap's alone — the local one is in `odom` and rolls with the robot.

**2. Slip and a wrong wheel radius.** If `/odom` says the robot drove 3.00 m and the tape says 2.85 m, everything downstream is 5 % wrong: AMCL fights the odometry, the controller's feedforward is off, and the robot consistently overshoots goals. Fix it where it belongs — calibration ([09.05](../09-odometry/09.05-calibrating-odometry.md)) — not in Nav2.

**3. Localization jitter.** AMCL jumping several centimetres while standing still makes every short-lookahead controller weave and every tight goal tolerance unreachable. First check whether the map is good ([11.09](../11-slam/11.09-slam-troubleshooting.md)) and whether the room has features (a long blank corridor is the classic case); only then raise the tolerance.

**4. A starved CPU.** The symptoms are a controller loop that misses its rate, bond timeouts that take the whole stack down ([12.06](12.06-nav2-architecture.md)) and a robot that reacts late. In order of how much they buy back per unit of regret: turn the camera off while navigating, halve `amcl.max_particles` (karmel is already at 1000/200 instead of 2000/500), reduce the local costmap to 2 × 2 m at 5 Hz (already done), and only then lower `controller_frequency`.

### Level 5 — The tuning calculator

`tuning.py` turns measurements into a list of changes. A healthy robot gets almost none:

```bash
python 12-navigation/code/tuning.py
```

```text
recommendations for your measurements Measurements(scan_hz=10.0, controller_hz=20.0, amcl_std_m=0.02, …)
  FollowPath.transform_tolerance                            0.2 -> 0.3      3 periods of the slowest input (10.0 Hz)
```

A robot in trouble gets a specific, ordered list:

```bash
python 12-navigation/code/tuning.py --door 0.62 --scan-hz 6 --controller-hz 11 \
       --amcl-std 0.07 --cpu 0.92 --max-speed 0.19
```

```text
  controller_server.general_goal_checker.xy_goal_tolerance     0.15 -> 0.28     2 sigma AMCL (7 cm) + overshoot
  FollowPath.transform_tolerance                            0.2 -> 0.5      3 periods of the slowest input (6.0 Hz)
  controller_server.controller_frequency                   20.0 -> 11       the loop is already missing its rate
  amcl.max_particles                                       1000 -> 500      CPU load 92%: halve the cheapest thing first
  amcl.update_min_d                                        0.15 -> 0.3      fewer filter updates per metre buys back CPU
  FollowPath.desired_linear_vel                            0.25 -> 0.19     the robot cannot reach the commanded cruise speed
```

Every line has the measurement that justifies it. That is the deliverable of this lesson: not a tuned robot, a *justified* one.

## Code

[`code/tuning.py`](code/tuning.py) (tested by [`code/test_tuning.py`](code/test_tuning.py)) is the calculator: `Doorway`, `corner_cut_m`, `StopBudget`, `min_local_costmap_width_m`, `goal_tolerance_m`, `transform_tolerance_s`, the sim-vs-real table, and `recommend(Measurements)`, which compares karmel's shipped `nav2_params.yaml` with what you measured.

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class StopBudget:
    """Where the distance between "the obstacle appears" and "the robot is still" goes."""

    speed_m_s: float
    decel_m_s2: float
    sensor_period_s: float
    costmap_period_s: float
    controller_period_s: float

    @property
    def blind_m(self) -> float:
        return self.speed_m_s * (self.sensor_period_s + self.costmap_period_s + self.controller_period_s)

    @property
    def braking_m(self) -> float:
        return self.speed_m_s ** 2 / (2.0 * self.decel_m_s2)
```

```bash
python 12-navigation/code/tuning.py                                   # karmel's numbers
python 12-navigation/code/tuning.py --door 0.72 --scan-hz 5.5 --amcl-std 0.06 --cpu 0.9
python -m pytest 12-navigation/code                                   # the module's tests
```

It reads the real parameter file through [`code/nav2_config.py`](code/nav2_config.py), so its "current" column is whatever your workspace actually ships — edit `nav2_params.yaml`, re-run, and the recommendations change.

(b) The narrowest door karmel can pass at all, and the narrowest it can pass with 10 cm of margin on each side. (c) Stopping distance at 0.25 m/s with a **6 Hz** LiDAR, a 5 Hz local costmap and a 12 Hz controller — and how much of it is latency. ### Exercise 12.08-E4 — The first autonomous errand `[hardware]`

Hardware: `robot-base`, `lidar`. In this order, and not skipping any of it: wheels on a stand, watchdog test (kill the navigation process while driving, confirm the wheels stop); then on the floor with `desired_linear_vel: 0.15`, a 1 m goal in open space, hand on the power switch; then a 3 m goal in the same room; then a goal through a doorway. Record for each: result, time, recoveries, final pose error. Stop and diagnose at the first failure instead of trying the next goal.
**Simulation alternative:** the same ladder of goals in the apartment world, plus a written note of what you would do differently with a real robot at each rung.

### Exercise 12.08-E5 — Find your own doorway problem `[debugging]`

Hardware: `robot-base`, `lidar` (simulation alternative: the apartment world). Send a goal through your narrowest doorway. If it works, make it fail on purpose: raise the global `obstacle_max_range` to 5.0, or `inflation_radius` to 0.7, or `footprint_padding` to 0.1. What do `/global_costmap/static_layer` and `/global_costmap/obstacle_layer` look like at the door? Write the one-line cause for each of the three.

### Exercise 12.08-E6 — Design for a different robot `[design]`

A friend has a 45 × 40 cm robot with a 40 cm wheelbase, a 15 Hz LiDAR, a 1.0 m/s top speed, 1.2 m/s² of braking and a Jetson Orin Nano. Their flat has 75 cm doors. Produce their `nav2_params.yaml` diff against karmel's: footprint, inscribed radius, inflation radius and scaling, local costmap size, controller frequency, lookahead, goal tolerance, and whether they should use RPP or MPPI. Show the calculation for each, and name the one measurement you would insist on before they run it.

## Expected result

- **12.08-E1:** (a) Corridor $0.62 - 0.23 = 0.39$ m; centre cost $\lfloor 252 e^{-5(0.31-0.115)}\rfloor = \lfloor 252 \times 0.377\rfloor = 95$. (b) Geometrically, anything wider than $2r = 0.23$ m; with 10 cm of margin per side, $0.23 + 0.20 = 0.43$ m — but a 43 cm door leaves no room for localization error, so in practice 60 cm is the sensible floor. (c) Latency $1/6 + 1/5 + 1/12 = 0.45$ s → blind 11.3 cm, braking 3.9 cm, total 15.2 cm, of which 74 % is latency. (d) $2(0.06) + 0.113 + 0.03 = 0.26$ m. (e) Clearance per side is 19.5 cm, so $L \le 0.195/0.293 = 0.67$ m — and you would not go near that: half of it, 0.3 m, leaves real margin. `tuning.py` recommends `xy_goal_tolerance` 0.26, `transform_tolerance` 0.5 and `controller_frequency` 12 for those inputs.
- **12.08-E2:** `max_particles: 1000` and `update_min_d: 0.15` are the compute ones (a Pi 5 running AMCL beside everything else; fewer particles and fewer updates per metre both buy CPU, at the cost of a noisier pose). `local_costmap.width: 2` follows from the 12.7 cm stopping distance plus margin (0.9 m needed, 2 m given). `inflation_radius: 0.35` and `cost_scaling_factor: 5.0` follow from the 80 cm doorways: a steeper fall-off keeps the doorway cheap while still pushing the path away from walls in open space. `desired_linear_vel: 0.25` is the course's safety limit for a robot in a home, below the 0.3 m/s the smoother allows and well below the 0.5 m/s the hardware could do. `default_server_timeout: 200` is an empirical fix: at the default 20 ms, goals abort on a loaded Pi or a CPU-rendered simulation (recorded in TESTED.md). Wrong in the other direction: too few particles → AMCL loses the robot after a bump; too small a local costmap → the robot sees obstacles too late; too large an inflation radius → doorways become expensive and the robot crawls; too high a cruise speed → every latency number above doubles.
- **12.08-E3:** A realistic first set on a Pi 5 with an RPLIDAR C1: scan 9–10 Hz, controller 18–20 Hz, AMCL σ 2–5 cm, TF age 30–80 ms, doors 70–80 cm, actual speed 0.22–0.25 m/s, CPU 50–75 %. That set produces at most one or two recommendations — usually `transform_tolerance`. If your measurements are much worse than this, the fix is upstream (a bad map, a loose LiDAR mount, a Pi throttling on a weak supply), not in `nav2_params.yaml`. The simulation gets the LiDAR rate, the odometry accuracy and the obstacle content optimistically wrong; its "CPU" is your laptop's and tells you nothing about the Pi.
- **12.08-E4:** The 1 m open-space goal should succeed first time with 0 recoveries and a final error within the 15 cm tolerance. The doorway goal is the one that finds your problems: expect either success, or `NO_VALID_PATH` (208) from a closed-up costmap, or a slow crawl from cost-regulated speed scaling. All three are diagnosed with the procedure of [12.07](12.07-nav2-in-simulation.md), Level 5.
- **12.08-E5:** `obstacle_max_range: 5.0` → 208, and `/compute_path_to_pose` fails too; the obstacle layer shows a smeared second wall a few centimetres off the static one. `inflation_radius: 0.7` → the goal usually still succeeds, but slowly: inflation never blocks, it makes the corridor expensive, and RPP's cost regulation reads that cost as "close to an obstacle". `footprint_padding: 0.1` → inscribed radius 0.205 m, corridor $0.8 - 0.41 = 0.39$ m; narrow doors start returning 208 and `GOAL_OCCUPIED` (206) appears for goals near walls. The lesson: *two* of the three do not block anything and still ruin the behavior.
- **12.08-E6:** Footprint `[[0.225, 0.20], [0.225, -0.20], [-0.225, -0.20], [-0.225, 0.20]]`, inscribed 0.20 m. A 75 cm door gives a corridor of $0.75 - 0.40 = 0.35$ m — tight, so `cost_scaling_factor` must be at least 5 and preferably higher, `inflation_radius` around 0.45 m, and `lookahead_dist` at most $0.175/0.293 = 0.60$ m, realistically 0.3–0.4. At 1.0 m/s with 1.2 m/s² and a 15 Hz LiDAR: latency $\approx 0.067 + 0.2 + 0.05 = 0.32$ s → blind 32 cm, braking 42 cm, total 74 cm, so the local costmap needs to be at least $2(0.74 + 0.3) \approx 2.1$ m — 3 × 3 m is the sensible choice. Controller 20–30 Hz; the Orin can run MPPI, and at 1 m/s its smoothness is worth having. The measurement to insist on: the AMCL pose noise, because at 1 m/s a 35 cm corridor leaves no room for a localizer that jitters.

## Troubleshooting

### Symptom: everything worked in simulation and nothing works on the robot

1. `use_sim_time`. Check every node: `ros2 param get /controller_server use_sim_time` and so on for AMCL, the costmaps and `bt_navigator`. One `true` poisons the whole TF tree.
2. Is `/scan` actually publishing, at what rate, and in which frame? `ros2 topic hz /scan`, `ros2 topic echo --once /scan --field header`.
3. `ros2 run tf2_ros tf2_monitor map base_footprint` — is the chain complete, and how old is the newest transform?

### Symptom: the robot drives well in the open and refuses to go through doors

1. Compute the corridor: door width − 2 × inscribed radius. Under about 30 cm, no amount of tuning helps; reduce `footprint_padding` or accept that the door is too narrow.
2. Look at the two global costmap layers separately at the door ([12.07](12.07-nav2-in-simulation.md), Level 5). Shorten the global `obstacle_max_range` before touching anything else.
3. Check the map itself at the door: SLAM often thickens door frames ([11.09](../11-slam/11.09-slam-troubleshooting.md)).
4. Only then look at `lookahead_dist` and the corner cut.

### Symptom: the robot weaves along straight walls

1. AMCL jitter: echo `/amcl_pose` while standing still. More than 3–4 cm of σ and every controller will weave.
2. Lookahead too short for the real latency: raise `lookahead_dist`, or enable `use_velocity_scaled_lookahead_dist` (karmel does).
3. Wheel velocity loop: commanded versus measured wheel speeds ([08.09](../08-control/08.09-feedforward-exact-speed.md)). A slow inner loop looks like a controller problem and is not.

### Symptom: Nav2 shuts itself down after a minute on the Pi

1. Bond timeout ([12.06](12.06-nav2-architecture.md)): the `lifecycle_manager` log names the unresponsive server.
2. Measure CPU per thread (`top -H`) before changing a parameter. The usual culprits are the camera, AMCL particles and, if you switched to it, MPPI.
3. Check the power supply and thermals: a throttled Pi 5 looks exactly like a CPU shortage, because it is one.

### Symptom: the robot consistently overshoots or undershoots goals

1. Odometry calibration first ([09.05](../09-odometry/09.05-calibrating-odometry.md)): drive 3 m, measure, compare with `/odom`.
2. Then the approach behavior: `approach_velocity_scaling_dist` and `min_approach_linear_velocity`, and the coasting analysis in [12.05](12.05-local-planning-obstacle-avoidance.md).
3. A goal tolerance tighter than your AMCL noise looks like an overshoot problem and is not.

## Common mistakes

- **Copying a TurtleBot's parameters.** Different radius, different speed, different CPU — every one of the numbers above changes.
- **Changing parameters before measuring.** You cannot tell which change helped.
- **Changing more than one at a time.** Same reason, twice as expensive.
- **Tuning Nav2 to fix odometry or a bad map.** Fix it where it is broken.
- **Leaving `use_sim_time: true` on one node.**
- **Testing the first autonomous run on the floor.** Stand, then floor, then doorway.
- **Trusting `cancelTask()` or a keyboard interrupt as a stop.** The watchdog and the collision monitor are what stop the robot.
- **Tuning in an empty room.** The robot lives with furniture, rugs and a cat; tune where it will drive.

## Knowledge check

1. karmel's inflated inscribed radius is 11.5 cm. What is the narrowest doorway it can plan through, and what is the narrowest you should actually ask it to?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   Geometrically anything wider than 23 cm, since cells within the inscribed radius of an obstacle are cost 253 and planners refuse them. In practice you want 10 cm of margin per side for localization error and control error, so about 45 cm is the floor and 60 cm is comfortable.
   </details>

2. At 0.25 m/s, which is larger for karmel — the blind distance or the braking distance? What does that imply?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   Blind: 8.8 cm against 3.9 cm of braking, because latency is 350 ms. It implies that a faster sensor or a faster costmap update buys more safety than stronger brakes, and that the local costmap size is set by latency, not by the brakes.
   </details>

3. Your AMCL pose jitters by σ = 7 cm standing still. Give two parameter consequences and one thing you should fix instead.
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   `xy_goal_tolerance` must be about 0.28 m (2σ + overshoot + margin), and a short `lookahead_dist` will weave, so raise it or use velocity scaling. What you should actually fix: the map or the environment — a featureless corridor, a bad SLAM map, or a LiDAR mounted where it sees mostly the robot itself.
   </details>

4. Why should the **global** costmap's `obstacle_max_range` be shorter than the **local** one's?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   The global costmap is in the `map` frame, so every marked point carries the localization error and stays until something raytraces it away; far marks land off the true walls and close doorways. The local costmap is in `odom`, rolls with the robot, is small and is rebuilt several times a second, so errors leave it quickly.
   </details>

5. Predict: you double `desired_linear_vel` from 0.25 to 0.5 m/s and change nothing else. Name three things that get worse, with numbers.
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   Stopping distance goes from 12.7 to 33.1 cm (latency doubles, braking quadruples). The replanning interval of 1 Hz now covers 50 cm of travel instead of 25. And the velocity-scaled lookahead grows (0.5 × 1.5 s = 0.75 m, clamped at 0.8), so the corner cut goes from about 12 cm to 23 cm — more than the clearance in a 60 cm door.
   </details>

6. What stops karmel's wheels if the Raspberry Pi loses power mid-goal? And if your Python process is killed?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   Power loss: nothing needs to act — the Pico loses its commands and its 300 ms watchdog stops the motors, and in any case the motor driver has no power source of its own once the pack is switched off. A killed Python process: Nav2 keeps driving; the robot stops only when `diff_drive_controller`'s `cmd_vel` timeout, the collision monitor or the Pico watchdog acts. Your script is not a stop.
   </details>

7. Your controller logs "Control loop missed its desired rate" ten times a minute on the Pi. What do you measure, and what do you change last?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   Measure CPU per thread and check for thermal throttling and a weak supply first. Then reduce work: camera off while navigating, fewer AMCL particles, a smaller local costmap, RPP instead of MPPI. `controller_frequency` is the *last* thing to lower — it is tuning the robot to the computer rather than fixing the computer.
   </details>

8. Why does this lesson insist on a written diff rather than an edited file?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   Because every line must be traceable to a measurement, and because you must be able to revert exactly one change when the robot gets worse. A rewritten file is untestable: you cannot tell which of twenty changes caused today's behavior.
   </details>

## Practical challenge

Produce a **tuning report** for karmel in your own home, and a `nav2_params.yaml` diff of at most eight lines.

1. Measure all six numbers plus CPU, in the room, with the robot driving. Include how you measured each.
2. Run `tuning.py` with your measurements and record the recommendations.
3. Define a fixed test: three goals (open space, across the room, through your narrowest doorway), each run three times from the same start pose. Record result, time, recoveries and final pose error — 27 runs in all if you do it properly for baseline and final.
4. Apply changes **one at a time**, re-running the test after each, and keep a log: parameter, old, new, the measurement behind it, and what happened to the numbers.
5. Revert anything that did not help, and explain why you thought it would.
6. Finish with: the diff, the before/after table, and the one thing that would have to change if karmel drove at 0.5 m/s.

**Acceptance criteria:** every line of the diff has a measurement and a calculation behind it; the before/after table shows the same goals from the same start poses; at least one change was reverted, with an explanation; the report names which failure was *not* a Nav2 problem (there is almost always one — a map, the odometry, a mount); and you can say what the numbers would look like if you re-ran the whole thing in a different room.

> [!CAUTION]
> **Safety:** this challenge is dozens of autonomous runs. Keep the speed at or below 0.25 m/s, keep the test area clear, keep a hand near the switch for the first run of every new parameter set, and never leave the robot navigating unattended — especially not near stairs, which karmel's 2D LiDAR at 16.5 cm cannot see ([SAFETY.md](../SAFETY.md), [12.10](12.10-recovery-and-navigation-safety.md)).

## Go deeper

- Nav2 first-time robot setup guide (Jazzy): https://docs.nav2.org/jazzy/configuration_and_development/first_time_robot_setup_guide/ — TF, URDF, odometry, sensors and footprint, in the order a new robot needs them.
- Nav2 tuning guide (Jazzy): https://docs.nav2.org/jazzy/configuration_and_development/tuning_guide/ — inflation, costmaps, controller and planner tuning, by the maintainers.
- Nav2 costmap 2D parameters: https://docs.nav2.org/jazzy/configuration_and_development/configuration_guide/core_servers/costmap_2d/ — `obstacle_max_range`, `raytrace_max_range`, `footprint_padding`, `track_unknown_space`.
- Nav2 AMCL parameters: https://docs.nav2.org/jazzy/configuration_and_development/configuration_guide/others/configuring_amcl/ — `max_particles`, `update_min_d`, the motion-model alphas.
- Macenski et al., "From the Desks of ROS Maintainers: A Survey of Modern & Capable Mobile Robotics Algorithms in ROS 2" (2023): https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.15236 — what people actually deploy, and on what compute.
- [`labs/ros2_ws/TESTED.md`](../labs/ros2_ws/TESTED.md) — the verification log for this workspace, including the two real-robot paths against a fake Pico and the findings that were fixed.
